products exactly as shipped; coloured bars are our constructions at their best single
cut. The geography null (0.128) lands inside the product range, while flat voting
(0.290) and weighted fusion (0.343) reach more than twice the best single product,
which is where the products' real value shows
(@sec-dial).](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_best_f1_r10.png){#fig-bestf1}

## The expert reference is a floor, so every precision is an interval {#sec-floor}

**Result.** Checked against the field reports, Copernicus EMS captured 94% of destroyed
buildings but only 49% of those significantly damaged (@fig-gradeslope): the expert map
is thorough about destruction and patchy about everything short of it, and the products
inherit the same slope. Crediting the flags that crowd reviewers confirmed as damaged
lifts Microsoft's precision from 0.08 to roughly 0.24, a factor of three that reflects
the reference, not the product. Some damage escaped everything: about 11% of
field-reported damage points, mostly in inland hill communities, had no flag from any
product within 20 m despite lying inside analysed extents. Taken together, though, the
products' combined recall is genuinely high: at least one of the six flagged within
20 m of 96% of field points in the core region.

**How it was measured.** The three references were turned on each other: field points
grade the expert reference's completeness by damage class; crowd verdicts re-judge the
flags the expert reference calls false; and every precision is then reported as an
interval from the expert-measured floor to the crowd-adjusted value. An independent
re-vote of the crowd campaign at three times the depth confirmed the adjustment's
stability (13.2% versus 11.5% of flags confirmed). The adjudication mechanics, their
granularity caveats, and the re-vote are in the Appendix.

![**Region: within the CEMS-analysed extents; reference: field reports (20 m GPS tolerance).** Recall by damage grade. Each line is one dataset's recall against
field-reported damage, at "complete" destruction versus "significant" damage. Every
line slopes down: the products and the expert reference alike find lighter damage far
less often, which is why measured recall is a ceiling and measured precision a
floor.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2e_grade_slope.png){#fig-gradeslope}

## Area ranking works, and geography ranks about as well {#sec-ranking}

**Result.** Ask which *neighbourhoods* to go to first, rather than which buildings, and
the picture improves a lot: at the ~5 km² sector scale the best products correctly
identify 80–85% of the twenty worst-hit cells, with rank correlations around 0.54–0.59.
This is the scale at which the products are genuinely usable. It is not, however, a
scale at which they demonstrate information beyond geography, and we tested that under
both of the paper's lenses (@fig-nullranking). As delivered, across everything each
product shipped, the hindsight geography model out-ranks five of the six. Read that
carefully, because 96% of the reference sits in one damage zone, so the as-delivered
task is largely "find the damage zone", which coast-plus-density solves almost by
definition. In the core region, where every product and the model score the identical
cells and the model therefore has a single score (0.65), the six split three–three:
LIST (0.74), IMPACT (0.72) and OSU (0.70) rank above it, Microsoft (0.61), UNEP (0.58)
and UH (0.48) below. So the products do carry real information about where within a
damage zone to go first; what they do not add is knowledge of which zone, the part
geography already encodes.

**How it was measured.** Flags and reference points are aggregated to hexagonal grid
cells and each product's ordering of cells is compared with the expert ordering by rank
correlation, with the geography model's expected damage count ranked the same way. In
the as-delivered test each comparison runs on the cells of that product's own footprint,
so the model is re-scored per row; in the core-region test all six products and the
model are scored on the identical shared cells, so the model has one value. The cell
lattices, full tables, and a priority map are in the Appendix.

![**Lenses: test 1 as delivered (each product's own footprint cells, so the model is
re-scored per row); test 2 the core region (one shared cell set, so the model has a
single score).** Both ranking tests: how well each product orders cells by damage
(grey) against the geography model on the same cells (red). As delivered the model
ranks better for five of six; in the core region the six split three–three around its
single score of
0.65.](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3f_null_ranking_both.png){#fig-nullranking}

## Agreement between independent products is the operating point {#sec-dial}

**Result.** The products fail in different places, so the number of them agreeing on a
building is informative, and it behaves as a dial with a known price at every setting
(@tbl-dial): from "any product" (97% of known damage, 26 visits per verified find) to
"all six" (crowd-adjusted precision 0.93, 18% of the damage). Counting agreement
roughly doubles the accuracy of the best single product (F1 0.290 against 0.148) and
requires no weights, no training data and no reference, so it is computable the hour
the second product lands. A statistically fitted fusion of the same inputs scores 18%
higher (0.343), but its weights come from the damage map a responder is still waiting
for: like the geography null, it explains the event afterwards and cannot run during
one.

| rule | flags | CEMS precision floor | crowd-adjusted precision | damage coverage (CEMS, 30 m) | visits per verified find (30 m) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1-of-6 (union) | 37,644 | 0.03 | 0.21 | 0.97 | 26.5 |
| 3-of-6 | 9,409 | 0.10 | 0.28 | 0.86 | 7.5 |
| 4-of-6 | 3,347 | 0.19 | 0.38 | 0.67 | 3.4 |
| 6-of-6 | 214 | 0.64 | 0.93 | 0.18 | 0.8 |

: **Lens: core region (61 km²).** The voting rules, priced. Two scales appear
by design: the precision columns use the strict 10 m building rule, while coverage and
visits-per-find use a 30 m line-of-sight scale (would a responder sent there *see* the
damage), which is the scale a wasted trip is actually judged at. {#tbl-dial}

The active ingredient is **independence of method, not diversity of sensors**. The
strongest two-product rule in the study pairs Microsoft with UH, the weakest product we
measured: both are optical, and they even share an imagery vendor, but they share no
model, and their failure zones sit at opposite ends of the study area, so each covers
for the other (@fig-frontier). The pair that shares its entire method, the two
Sentinel-1 coherence products, is the weakest of all fifteen pairings. What products
share (sensor, platform, model) is knowable without labels on day one, so the
transferable rule is: count agreement between *independent methods*.

Three qualifications keep this honest. Flat voting means trusting every product
equally, and that UH's full vote *helped* could only be established with a reference in
hand. Single products cannot be tuned out of their ceiling: same-sensor agreement,
confidence-score sweeps, and within-product corroboration all plateau well below the
cross-product rules (Appendix). And choosing the agreement threshold buys a workload,
not a hit rate: flag counts are observable on day one, the precision they deliver is
not. What this section implies for practice is collected in the Recommendations.

![**Lens: core region (61 km²).** The fifteen two-product rules. Pairing across independent methods lifts precision;
the pair sharing its entire method is the weakest of
all.](artefacts/RQ5-ensemble/figs/rq5b_frontier_r10.png){#fig-frontier}

## One failure could be traced; five could not be examined {#sec-casestudy}

**Result.** Microsoft's largest failure is a western strip where crowd reviewers judged
71% of its flags undamaged. Its published per-building metadata places that strip under
a single satellite scene, processed alone (@fig-weststrip); east of the boundary, where
scenes overlap, the same product's precision is four times higher (0.205 against
0.052). A vendor-level cross-check runs in the same direction: UH, whose authors
confirm it ran exclusively on imagery from the same vendor, flags only 3% of that strip
where Microsoft flags 32%. The failure is established to travel with the scene; whether
the cause was the image itself or the model's handling of it cannot be separated with
current data. Microsoft's own public report corroborates the mechanism from the
producer's side: it names the Catia La Mar overlap as its single largest source of
inter-scene disagreement, with the Vantor 25 June scene flagging ~2,600 buildings as
damaged that the Planet 26 June scene calls intact, resolved in overlap zones by
preferring the later Planet read. The strip in question is where no second scene was
available to overrule the first. Microsoft was the only product publishing metadata at
this granularity, which is why its failure is the only one that could be examined this
way.

**How it was measured.** The crowd campaign's verdicts were aggregated over the strip
and compared with the product's per-building scene counts and dates; an independent
second crowd campaign over the same cells later reproduced the confirmation side of the
verdict. Details, including what the re-vote could and could not re-test, are in the
Appendix.

![**Region: the western half of Microsoft's delivered strip (Catia La Mar).** The western strip. Top left: where Microsoft flags far more than the expert map
records. Bottom left: where crowd volunteers said nothing is there. Right: cell by cell
the two do not track; the agreement is at the scale of the strip, which sat under a
single satellite
scene.](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_west_cluster_adjudication.png){#fig-weststrip}

## Summary and discussion {#sec-discussion}

The three questions from the Introduction now have answers. *Can a responder act on a
single flagged building?* No: precision is 0.04–0.09 even in the best-mapped area, every
number measured against an incomplete reference is a floor, and no single product can
be tuned out of that ceiling. *Do the products rank neighbourhoods well enough to
triage?* Yes, and this is their genuinely usable scale; but a hindsight geography model
ranks about as well, so treat the ranking as useful rather than as evidence the product
saw something the map did not. *What is the sensible way to use them?* Count agreement
between independent methods. It is the only method we tested that is both effective
(roughly double any single product) and available during a response, and its price at
every setting is knowable in advance as a workload.

Two further results close tempting shortcuts. First, a product's reliability cannot be
judged from its own flags: across fifteen product-and-area combinations, nothing in the
flags' rate, clustering, or cross-product agreement predicted measured reliability
(every correlation statistically indistinguishable from zero). False alarms cluster the
way real damage clusters, so the map alone cannot tell a devastated neighbourhood from
a fooled model; judging reliability where no reference exists requires field reports, a
crowd, or a model trained on previous events. Second, and more encouraging: where a
reference does exist, failures can be *mapped*, not just measured. Across 78–86% of
each product's territory the errors scatter randomly, the harmless kind of wrong, and
the trouble concentrates in a few identifiable pockets, which suggests discounting each
product's vote inside its known bad pockets as a next step for fusion.

The strongest way to harden every claim here is replication, and a specific candidate
exists: the 2025 Myanmar earthquake has a comparable multi-product, crowd-validated
landscape. The method transfers as-is; whether the single-product ceiling, the monotone
ordering of the voting rules, and the grade gradient hold there is exactly what one
event cannot establish.

## Recommendations

The results imply changes in practice for three audiences. We collect them here, once.

::: {.callout-tip title="For responders"}
**Do not spend time choosing a product; spend it counting agreement between products.** On
this event no single product was meaningfully better than a model of coastline distance and
building density, but the number of products agreeing on a building roughly doubled the
accuracy of any of them alone. Unlike a fitted model, counting requires no weights, no
training data and no reference, so it can be done the hour the second product arrives. Weight
the count toward *independent methods*: products that share a sensing method fail together
and their agreement carried the least information in our tests, while products with nothing
in common but the event cover for each other's failure zones. Then set the threshold from
your own capacity (@tbl-dial gives the flag counts and visit costs at each level),
remembering that you are choosing a workload, not a guaranteed hit rate. Used at sector
scale, any major product ranks where to go first: trust that ranking, not the building
counts, while noting that coarse geography ranks about as well. Nothing in the current
ecosystem sees lighter damage reliably, so plan shelter assessments accordingly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For providers"}
Publish an analysed extent; without one, a product cannot be evaluated or safely used.
Publish per-building acquisition metadata (scene count and dates); those fields are what
allowed this paper to trace a failure to a single satellite scene. Surface corroboration
to users as a confidence tier rather than leaving it in an archive column. Validate where
the product is deployed, not where validation data happens to exist; the failing scene
here was the unvalidated one. Check new products against a geography-only baseline, which
every single product in this event merely tied. And accept feedback during the
activation: a crowd campaign rejected 71% of one zone's flags within days, and no channel
existed to carry that signal back while reprocessing could still help.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="For evaluators and coordinators"}
A single expert reference understates precision most where damage is lighter. Publish
measured precision as a lower bound, or better, adjudicate the disputed flags against a
second reference and publish the interval. Note that unanimous product agreement without
expert corroboration turned out to be mostly real damage, so consensus doubles as a
detector of reference gaps and a field-validation queue. Finally, coverage is an
ecosystem property: the inland communities missed by every product were inside analysed
extents, and nobody knew that nobody was seeing them. A shared, live picture of who is
looking where costs providers nothing and closes the one gap here that no amount of
fusion can.
:::

## Limitations

**One event, one geography, and mostly one neighbourhood.** This is a single earthquake
in a coastal, dense-urban setting, and the core comparison region is only ~61 km². More
restrictive still, 96% of the CEMS reference sits in a single AOI (Caraballeda), so every
pooled number is effectively that AOI's number. In the four low-damage AOIs, measured
precision (0.00–0.02) cannot distinguish product over-flagging from reference
incompleteness (@fig-peraoi). The specific rule orderings and magnitudes are hypotheses
elsewhere.

**The crowd and field references have limits of their own.** The crowd campaign was
seeded from two AI products' flags, so it scrutinises products unevenly and can never
see any product's misses; its volunteers are not damage-assessment experts, and their
verdicts are per ~50 m cell, not per building. The field reports are undated,
positives-only, skewed toward destruction, and come with no defined collection area, so
the inland-gap estimate is a lower bound.

**What we know about the products themselves is uneven.** The
independence-versus-shared-method contrast rests on a single same-method pair. UH's
exclusively-Vantor optical basis is author-confirmed; LIST's radar basis remains
provider-stated rather than documented, and input-imagery details and release dates for
both await provider confirmation. OSU's revised v1, delivered after the study window, is
used by the operational dashboard but enters this paper only in the version comparison
(Appendix); all other OSU numbers are v0.

**Voting inherits the shared footprint base.** Two products can fail to co-flag a
building for alignment reasons rather than genuine disagreement, so the recall of the
strict-agreement rules is understated.

**The geography null enjoys hindsight the products never had.** It is fitted to this
event's reference labels; although it is scored strictly on held-out buildings, it
carries an event-specific calibration no responder possessed. It is an upper bound on
geography-only skill, and the claim it supports is about information content, not about
what was operationally in hand. A model fitted on previous earthquakes, which is what a
responder would really have, would score somewhere below this bound and remains
untested.

**Pending work.** Bootstrap confidence intervals and population-weighted prioritisation
are in progress and absent from this draft. The timeliness axis is preliminary:
@fig-timeline reconstructs availability only, and the decision-relevant interaction of
accuracy with arrival date awaits confirmed provider-release dates.


## Appendix {.unnumbered}

The main text states each result with a summary of how it was measured; this
appendix carries the full machinery, inherited from the long-form draft
(`manuscript_v2`), which it supersedes.

### Matching products to references, in full {.unnumbered}

The product and reference use different geometries (CEMS drops points on damaged
buildings, while each product flags its own footprints on its own building base), so there
is no shared list of instances on which to build a single confusion matrix. We therefore
score by *proximity*, the standard approach for detection-style evaluation: precision
anchors on the product (of its flagged buildings, how many have a CEMS damage point within
radius r?), and recall anchors on the reference (of the CEMS damage points, how many have a
product flag within r?). Each metric carries its own denominator. Because the two metrics
are precision and recall, neither uses the undamaged background (true negatives), which we
could not enumerate anyway, since CEMS never labels the undamaged stock.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Dual-anchored matching. Left: a product is scored only where it AND the reference both looked. Middle: recall anchors on the reference; each CEMS damage point asks whether a product flag lies within radius r. Right: precision anchors on the product; each flagged building asks whether a CEMS point lies within r. Each metric brings its own denominator."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mp
import numpy as np
from shapely.geometry import Point

R = 0.16
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 5.1))
a0 = ax[0]
c1, c2 = Point(-0.28, 0).buffer(0.75), Point(0.28, 0).buffer(0.75)
inter = c1.intersection(c2)
a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(inter.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="#c8e6c9", ec="none"))
for c, col, lab, xy in ((c1, "tab:blue", "CEMS analysed extent", (-0.75, 0.62)),
                        (c2, "tab:orange", "product AOI", (0.42, 0.62))):
    a0.add_patch(mp.Polygon(np.asarray(c.exterior.coords), closed=True, fc="none", ec=col, lw=2))
    a0.annotate(lab, xy, fontsize=9, color=col)
a0.annotate("scored HERE only", (0, -0.05), fontsize=10, ha="center", weight="bold", color="#2e7d32")
a0.set_title("1 · where scoring happens", fontsize=10)
a1 = ax[1]
for x, y in [(-0.38, 0.22), (0.05, -0.32), (-0.6, -0.5), (0.62, -0.15)]:
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.3, True), (0.15, -0.25, True), (0.45, 0.42, False)]:
    a1.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a1.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
    a1.annotate("TP" if hit else "FN (missed)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a1.set_title("2 · RECALL — anchor on each CEMS point", fontsize=10)
a2 = ax[2]
for x, y in [(-0.36, 0.25), (0.2, -0.14)]:
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="*", s=180, c="k", zorder=4)
for x, y, hit in [(-0.45, 0.32, True), (0.1, -0.2, True), (0.5, 0.45, False), (-0.15, -0.6, False)]:
    a2.add_patch(mp.Circle((x, y), R, fc="none", ec="grey", ls="--"))
    a2.scatter(x, y, marker="s", s=70, c="tab:orange", zorder=3)
    a2.annotate("TP" if hit else "FP (false alarm)", (x + 0.05, y + 0.13), fontsize=9,
                color="#2e7d32" if hit else "#c62828", weight="bold")
a2.set_title("3 · PRECISION — anchor on each product flag", fontsize=10)
for a in ax:
    a.set_xlim(-1.05, 1.05); a.set_ylim(-1.0, 0.9)
    a.set_aspect("equal"); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
h = [plt.Line2D([], [], marker="*", ls="", ms=13, c="k", label="CEMS damage point"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], marker="s", ls="", ms=8, c="tab:orange", label="product-flagged building"),
     plt.Line2D([], [], ls="--", c="grey", label="match radius r")]
fig.legend(handles=h, loc="lower center", ncol=3, frameon=False, fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(rect=(0, 0.07, 1, 0.97))
plt.show()
```

A product is only accountable where both it and the reference actually looked, so all
scoring is restricted to the intersection of analysed extents; @fig-extents maps every
extent this paper scores against, and the core region they share. UNEP debris publishes no
extent. Based on its density across the study region, we make the explicit assumption
that it fully covers the ~61 km² core comparison region, the same logic used for its
stand-alone evaluation in fully enclosed administrative units.

An analysed extent says where a product looked, not whether it could see: cloud can hide
individual buildings inside a declared extent. A robustness check against the one
product that publishes per-building visibility found the effect negligible in this
event (details in the Appendix), so all products are scored without visibility
corrections; the check is impossible for the five that publish no such field.

The matching radius comes from the urban fabric rather than from convenience. The median
distance between neighbouring building centroids in the core region is 9.7 m, and 93% of
buildings have a neighbour within 20 m. We therefore use r = 10 m as the largest radius
at which "did the product flag this building" is still a meaningful question. Larger
radii answer a different and equally legitimate question, namely whether the flag put a
responder within sight of real damage. We use named scales for those: 30 m (line of
sight), 60 m (same block), 100 m (right area).

**One matching rule, two labelled exceptions.** Every CEMS-based precision and recall in
this paper uses the 10 m radius, so all of them are directly comparable. Two labelled
exceptions appear later, each because it answers a different question: the coverage and
visits-per-find columns of the voting table use 30 m, the line-of-sight scale ("would a
responder sent here *see* the damage"), and recall against the ChatMap ground reports
uses 20 m, absorbing phone-GPS error in field-collected points. Both are restated where
they are used. (That field-matching 20 m is unrelated to the 20 m *label radius* of the
Appendix sensitivity re-run, which is an alternative definition of the target itself.)

Separately from the matching radius, results are reported in one of two *regions*, and
numbers are comparable only within one:

| reporting region | what it is | used for |
|---|---|---|
| **Core region** | the ~61 km² intersection of the CEMS extents with all five extent-publishing products (@fig-extents): one shared cell set | voting, the pairwise rules, fusion, and the best-F1 geography comparison |
| **As delivered** | each product's full delivered footprint, wherever CEMS mapped: a different region per product | the as-delivered scorecard and geography benchmark; ranking test 1 |

: The two reporting lenses. Sections and captions state which they use. The core
region gives every predictor an identical cell set (one geography score); as-delivered
is per-product by design, so the geography model is re-scored on each product's own
footprint there. {#tbl-regions}

One point about what the radius *is*: it is not a tolerance applied to the products,
but the definition of the target every predictor is scored against:

> A building counts as damaged if a CEMS damage point lies within *r* metres of it.

Widening it changes the truth being chased, not the leniency of the scoring: at 20 m
the identical CEMS points label 2,733 core-region buildings damaged; at 10 m, 1,350.
The product-versus-geography comparison is mildly radius-dependent as a result, so the
whole analysis is re-run at 20 m and 30 m in the Appendix ("Performance versus
matching radius", @tbl-radii): every number rises with the radius, and no conclusion changes.

Two implementation details complete the picture. The fusion analysis, which needs a label
for every building rather than only the flagged ones, matches buildings to CEMS points by
centroid, while the headline scorecard matches on each product's native geometry; at the
same radius the two implementations agree to within 0.005 in precision for every product
(@tbl-frames, Appendix), so that choice is immaterial. The radius is the one choice that
moves numbers. Microsoft's precision is 0.080 at 10 m and 0.138 at 20 m: the same
product, the same flags, the same reference, two definitions of what counts as a hit.


### Area ranking and error structure: method {.unnumbered}

For questions about where damage is concentrated, we aggregate per-building flags to
hexagonal grid cells at two sizes, roughly 0.74 km² and 5.2 km² (the larger approximates
a triage sector), and compare each product's ranking of cells against the ranking implied
by CEMS, using rank correlation and top-k overlap.

Whether a ranking survives noisy per-building labels depends on how the noise is arranged
in space, so we test that directly. A regression suited to counts (Poisson) predicts each
cell's flag count from its CEMS damage count, with the cell's building stock built in as
the baseline so that "more flags because more buildings" cannot register as bias. What
remains (flagging above or below what the real damage explains) is then tested in two
ways: for whether it bunches together on the map rather than scattering (Moran's I, a
standard score for exactly this, with its significance judged by reshuffling the values
across the same cells many times, which controls for the shape of the built-up area
itself), and for correlation with variables that would corrupt a ranking, namely building
density, distance to the coast, and modelled shaking intensity.

Two further tests use the same cell lattice. The first asks whether a product's
reliability in an area can be predicted from its flag pattern alone (its flag rate, how
tightly its flags cluster, how much it agrees with the other products), by correlating
those signals with measured reliability across every product-and-area combination. The
second classifies each product's territory cell by cell, using local versions of the
same clustering score, into places where its errors scatter at random and places where
they pile up.


### Combining products, and adjudicating disagreements: method {.unnumbered}

For per-building questions, each product's flags are projected onto the shared Overture
footprint base and combined by voting. A building passes the "k-of-6" rule when at least
k of the six products flag it. Throughout the paper, k-of-6 names a rule, never a score.
Voting rules are scored exactly as single products are.

Because CEMS itself has gaps, precision measured against CEMS is a lower bound. A
reference gap can turn a correct flag into an apparent false positive, but never the
reverse, so the true precision lies at or above the measured value. We estimate how far
above by adjudication: for every flagged building with no CEMS point within 10 m, we look
up the MapSwipe majority verdict for its cell and count the share that volunteers judged
damaged. "Crowd-adjusted precision" adds those confirmed flags back to the numerator.
Each precision estimate in this paper is therefore an interval, from the CEMS-measured
lower bound to the crowd-adjusted value. One caveat sets the character of the upper end:
MapSwipe verdicts are per ~50 m cell, not per building (@fig-refarch), so a
crowd-confirmed flag means "damage somewhere in this cell," not "this building." The
crowd-adjusted value is therefore an *upper* estimate of building-level precision, and the
truth lies between it and the CEMS floor. The stability of that crowd verdict was itself
re-tested: an independent second crowd re-voted the same cells at three times the depth
after this paper's freeze and confirmed 11.5% of the same flags where the first crowd
confirmed 13.2%, so the upper estimates here sit slightly high; the mechanism and the
full re-test are in the Appendix (@fig-crowdmech). A second, independent check uses ChatMap instead:
because its field points are building-level, they can be unioned directly with the CEMS
points, which raises measured precision by a smaller, sharper 5–9% (the field data is
sparse, 415 points, but geometrically exact).

Recall has no such correction, and its bias runs the other way. Adjudication re-judges
flags; it cannot add the damage CEMS never recorded to recall's denominator: the crowd
saw only AI-flagged places, and the field reports are positives-only with no survey
frame, so the full denominator is unknowable. Because the reference over-represents
destruction, which is the damage class every product detects best, recall measured
against it is flattered rather than understated. The rule of thumb for this whole paper:
**against an incomplete reference, measured precision is a floor and measured recall is
a ceiling.** The grade-stratified field-frame measurements in @sec-floor quantify
how much the recall ceiling gives back.


### The geography null model and weighted fusion, in full {.unnumbered}

Two of this paper's constructions are models rather than products, and both are built the
same way. The **geography null model** exists to calibrate what the accuracy numbers mean:
it asks how much of the damage pattern could be recovered from coarse spatial structure
and shaking alone, so that a product's score can be read against something other than
zero. It uses three context variables computed per building, all available within hours
of any earthquake: distance to the coastline, local building density, and the shaking
intensity estimated by the USGS ShakeMap. From these it predicts which buildings carry
CEMS-recorded damage. It is validated by **spatial blocking**: the map is cut into ~5 km²
zones and the model is always scored on zones it was not trained on, because neighbouring
buildings resemble each other in both their features and their damage, and an ordinary
random split would leak that resemblance into an inflated score (@fig-dayzero-build).

A null is only meaningful if it is the *strongest* honest account of "just geography"; a
weak one would flatter the products by construction. We therefore fit it two ways: a
logistic regression (a standard statistical model that weighs the three variables) and a
random forest (a more flexible model built from many decision trees, able to capture
interactions between the variables). Whichever scores higher in a given analysis is the
one reported, and both are disclosed. Which of the two wins genuinely differs across the paper's
analysis layers; the full comparison and the reasons are in the Appendix (@tbl-learners).
Nothing about the fusion results depends on that choice.

We call it a *null model* rather than a baseline, and deliberately avoid naming it after
day zero, because the distinction is easy to blur and consequential. Its three inputs are genuinely
available on day zero; its fitted coefficients are not. Estimating them requires the very
damage labels a responder is waiting for, so the model cannot be run on the day it names. It
is not an alternative anyone could have deployed. What it provides instead is a reference
level (the standard role of a null model, like a majority-class or stratified-random
comparator), and because we allow it to be fitted with hindsight, it is a *generous* null. The
two directions therefore read differently. A product that beats it has demonstrated real
information beyond spatial structure, and the inference is strong precisely because the null
was given every advantage. A product that loses to it has flags placed no better than an
obvious retrospective geography prior, which is a serious finding about that product. It is
not, however, a claim that geography was an available substitute.

How much *event* information the null actually uses differs by analysis layer: in the
core region the shaking estimate barely varies and the model runs on static geography
alone, while across the delivered footprints shaking carries a quarter to a third of
its weight. The as-delivered comparison is consequently the better founded of the two,
and the core-region comparison should be read strictly as a null (the Appendix carries
the detail).

The model's output is not a flag list but a continuous risk score per building. Every
cutoff on the score is a different flag list, so the model traces a whole curve of
precision–recall trade-offs, while a product, whose provider already fixed the
threshold, is a single point in that plane; the two are compared point-against-curve.
**Average precision**, the area under that curve, is reported only for continuous
scores; a shipped product is compared at its operating point instead (the Appendix
shows why a one-list "average precision" would mislead).

The **weighted fusion** is the same construction with the six products' flags and
confidence fields added to the three context variables: the geography null is exactly
this model with the product inputs removed. Both are refit for each analysis they
appear in, always under the same blocked validation. One caution: the learned weights
are calibrated to this single event and should not be assumed to transfer.

Two questions of fairness follow from putting a fitted model beside an unfitted product,
and both have short answers. Are they scored on the same data? Yes: the validation folds
partition the buildings, every building is scored by a model that never saw it, so
models and products face identical building sets with identical denominators (the
threshold-selection mechanics are in the Appendix). Is the model advantaged by
hindsight? Yes, deliberately: it is fitted to this event's reference labels, so it is an
**upper bound on geography-only skill for this event**, and the claim it supports is
about information content (the products add little beyond what three context variables
carry), never the operational claim that responders held such a model on day zero. The
Limitations return to this.

![How the geography null model is built. Three context variables known within hours of the
earthquake (coast distance, building density, and ShakeMap intensity) feed one
spatially-blocked model whose target is CEMS damage; both learners are fitted and the
stronger one is reported (the logistic here, the forest across the larger delivered
footprints of @sec-floor). Its output is a *continuous* per-building risk, so every
threshold on it is a different flag list and the score traces an entire precision–recall
curve, against which a single product is one already-thresholded point. No satellite
product enters this model. Note what the diagram cannot show: fitting it requires the
damage labels themselves, which is why it is a retrospective null rather than something
available on the day its inputs
are.](artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/figs/rq8_dayzero_schematic.png){#fig-dayzero-build}


### Area-ranking detail: tables and error structure {.unnumbered}

Because area ranking is the products' strongest result, it deserves the same null test as the
building-level numbers (the first of this paper's three product-versus-geography
comparisons; @tbl-nulltally collects all three). We summed the geography model's predicted per-building risk (each
building's risk always taken from a model fit that had never seen its neighbourhood)
over exactly the cells used above, giving an expected damage count per cell that needs no
threshold,
and correlated those with the CEMS count the same way:

| scale | product | ρ product | ρ geography null | difference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~5 km² (res 7) | Microsoft | 0.585 | **0.631** | -0.046 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | OSU | **0.540** | 0.485 | +0.055 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | IMPACT v2 | 0.433 | **0.673** | -0.240 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | LIST | 0.404 | **0.500** | -0.096 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | UNEP | 0.220 | **0.501** | -0.281 |
| ~5 km² (res 7) | UH | -0.085 | **0.701** | -0.786 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | OSU | **0.505** | 0.478 | +0.027 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | Microsoft | 0.466 | **0.568** | -0.102 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | IMPACT v2 | 0.292 | **0.594** | -0.303 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | LIST | 0.276 | **0.445** | -0.169 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | UNEP | 0.068 | **0.451** | -0.383 |
| ~0.7 km² (res 8) | UH | -0.114 | **0.580** | -0.694 |

: How well each ranking matches the expert damage count per cell (rank correlation,
Spearman's ρ): each product against the geography model, on identical cells within that
product's shared region. The two scales are hexagonal grid cells of roughly 5 km² ("res
7") and 0.7 km² ("res 8"). Only OSU exceeds the geography model, at either scale.
{#tbl-nullrank}

The result is uncomfortable but clear: **geography alone ranks these areas better than the
products do**, beating five of the six at the sector scale and five of six again at the finer
scale. The margins are not marginal (IMPACT 0.673 against 0.433, UNEP 0.501 against 0.220),
and UH's rank correlation is *negative* (−0.085), meaning its sector ordering is slightly worse
than no information at all. Only OSU is ahead of the null, and only narrowly (0.540 against
0.485).

That comparison spans all five mapped areas, however, and 96% of the reference damage sits in
one of them. Much of what it rewards is therefore the coarse discrimination of Caraballeda from
four quiet AOIs, a task coastline distance and building density solve almost by definition. The
sharper question is whether the products can out-rank geography *within* the damage zone, and
there the picture is different. Restricting every region to Caraballeda and re-running at
~0.7 km² cells, the six split evenly (@tbl-nullrank-cara): LIST, OSU and IMPACT beat the
null; Microsoft, UNEP and UH fall below it; and at ~0.1 km² the same three–three split
holds. **So the products do carry real information about where within a damaged area to
go first: what they do not add is knowledge of which area that is**, which is the part
geography already encodes. The headline five-of-six should be read as a statement about the
coarse task, not as evidence that the products are uninformative at every scale.

| product | ρ product | ρ geography null | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| LIST | 0.668 | 0.543 | +0.125 |
| IMPACT v2 | 0.548 | 0.456 | +0.092 |
| OSU | 0.642 | 0.562 | +0.080 |
| UNEP | 0.451 | 0.524 | -0.074 |
| Microsoft | 0.466 | 0.568 | -0.102 |
| UH | 0.389 | 0.597 | -0.208 |

: The same test restricted to the Caraballeda AOI, ~0.7 km² cells. Within the damage
zone the six split evenly against the null, and the same three-three split holds at
~0.1 km². {#tbl-nullrank-cara}

The interpretation carries the caveat already stated: the null is hindsight-fitted
(@sec-null), so this says the damage pattern was largely recoverable from geography
*after the fact*, not that a responder had this ranking on day one. What it does rule
out is the reading that area ranking demonstrates the products are extracting damage
information the geography does not already contain. At this
scale they are reproducing a spatial pattern, competently, that was largely predictable from
the map.

The error-structure test explains why ranking survives. The residual over-flagging is
strongly clustered in space (Moran's I 0.45–0.60, p = 0.001 for each of the three
products this test covers: Microsoft, IMPACT, and OSU, the members whose extents
overlap CEMS broadly enough for the cell-level regression; extending it to the newer
members is open work), so the errors are not random noise. But once building stock is controlled, the clustering
follows the earthquake itself: residuals rise toward the coast and with modelled shaking,
and show no association with building density. The specific worry that flags merely
reproduce the building map finds no support once building stock is controlled. In short,
the products over-call most where damage is genuinely worst. That error structure
preserves area rankings. The dangerous alternative, errors that track urban form, is what
the test rules out.

![Where each product over-flags once its building stock is accounted for (red = more
flags than the recorded damage explains), for the three products the error-structure test
covers. Each panel autoscales
to its own analysed region, which is why they look so different: Microsoft analysed a
single ~30 km coastal strip, so its few hundred grid cells appear as individual dots,
while IMPACT and OSU are Sentinel-1 swaths spanning roughly 200 km, whose thousands of
cells merge visually. IMPACT and OSU residuals follow the coastal severity gradient.
Microsoft's error is a single hard cluster at the west end of its
region.](artefacts/RQ3-prioritization-error-structure/figs/rq3_residual_maps_res8.png)

The same cell lattice yields two results that the Discussion takes up. First, nothing in
a product's own flag pattern predicts how reliable it is: across the fifteen
product-and-area combinations, no correlation between the pattern signals (flag rate,
clustering, agreement with other products) and measured reliability was statistically
distinguishable from zero. Second, mapping each product's errors cell by cell, 78–86% of
each product's territory shows errors scattered at random (noise rather than bias), with
the failures concentrated in a few identifiable pockets; Microsoft's western strip,
taken up in @sec-casestudy, is the largest.

One product does not fit this benign pattern. Microsoft's residual error is not a
gradient but a single dense cluster in the western coastal strip, and no covariate
explains it. At this point in the analysis we cannot say what the cluster is: real
over-detection and a local gap in the reference would look identical. Section
@sec-casestudy resolves the question with the other two references.

That ambiguity applies to every number in this section, not just the anomaly. Everything
above assumes CEMS is complete within its extents. The next section tests that
assumption.


### The scorecard in both frames, in full {.unnumbered}

**The pooled scorecard is one place's scorecard.** That cautionary tale generalizes,
and it bounds every headline number in this paper. CEMS activated five separate AOIs,
but 96% of its damage points sit in one of them: Caraballeda (1,468 points, against 26
in Morón, 14 in San Felipe, and 3 each in Caracas and Santa Cruz). Splitting the
scorecard by AOI (@fig-peraoi) shows two things. First, the pooled numbers *are*
Caraballeda's numbers: the per-AOI Caraballeda row reproduces the headline scorecard
almost exactly. Second, outside Caraballeda every product keeps flagging at scale
(IMPACT marks 9,445 buildings in the Caracas AOI, UH marks 32,145, 27.5% of the stock,
in Santa Cruz) while measured precision collapses to 0.00–0.02 everywhere. We state
plainly what those zeros can and cannot mean. They are floors against a reference that
recorded almost nothing in those AOIs, so two explanations are confounded: the products
hallucinating where damage is sparse (the same low-damage-zone mechanism as the UH
agricultural case and the Microsoft west strip), and CEMS under-recording damage in
AOIs it mapped thinly. The crowd cannot arbitrate here: the MapSwipe campaign
concentrated on the coastal strip, and at most 12% of these out-of-Caraballeda flags
fall on voted cells. Recall is measurable only in Morón (26 points), where the best
product finds 19% of it. What survives the ambiguity is the conditional: every
performance claim in this paper describes dense-damage coastal terrain, and in the four
low-damage AOIs the products' flags are almost entirely uncorroborated by any reference
we have.

Pooling all five AOIs gives the *as-delivered* scorecard: the product as a responder
received it, junk zones included. As-delivered precision: Microsoft 0.081, OSU 0.036,
IMPACT 0.032, UNEP 0.027, LIST 0.026, UH 0.009. Two things stand out. UH's number is
ten times worse than its best-case 0.093, because most of its flags sit in the
low-damage AOIs (32,145 in Santa Cruz alone). And Microsoft's number is *unchanged*,
not because its model behaves differently, but because it only published flags for the
coastal strip it had analysed carefully. Restraint in coverage is itself a product
property: shipping fewer, better-scoped zones protected Microsoft's as-delivered
precision, while shipping everywhere destroyed UH's.

Two mechanisms make the as-delivered numbers what they are, and both are worth stating
because they answer the obvious objection: *shouldn't precision be destroyed outside the
one dense zone?* The first is arithmetic. Because the four low-damage AOIs record almost no
damage, precision there is essentially zero, and the pooled figure is a flag-weighted
average, so a product's as-delivered precision falls by almost exactly the share of its
flags that land outside Caraballeda: Microsoft 0% of flags and 0% lost, OSU 17% and 16%,
IMPACT and LIST 52% and 52%, UNEP 68% and 68%, UH 90% and 90% (every product lands on the
diagonal *precision lost = share of flags in the dead zones*; plotted in @fig-deadzone,
in the Appendix). Precision is not *resisting* the false alarms; it collapses in direct
proportion to where each product chose to flag. The second mechanism means even this understates the problem: the
as-delivered frame can only score flags that fall inside a CEMS extent, and most products
flag far beyond one. Of each product's total flags, the share landing outside every CEMS
extent (where no reference can score them at all) is 4% for Microsoft but 43% for OSU,
71% for IMPACT, 76% for UNEP, and 79% for LIST. Since damage was concentrated on the coast,
the bulk of those unscoreable flags are almost certainly false positives. So every precision
figure in this paper, as-delivered included, is measured on each product's most favourable,
reference-covered subset; the true precision across a product's full output is very likely
lower, and unmeasurably so.

The as-delivered frame also re-runs this paper's harshest benchmark (the second of the
three product-versus-geography comparisons of @tbl-nulltally). We trained the
geography null model (coast distance, building density, and ShakeMap intensity,
constructed as described in @sec-null) on each product's full delivered footprint
under the same spatially blocked validation, then had it flag exactly as many buildings
as that product shipped, taking its highest-risk buildings first. Compared this way,
list against list at each product's own delivered size, **four of the six products are
matched or beaten by the geography model on both precision and recall** (pairs below
read precision / recall): IMPACT 0.032 / 0.55 against the model's 0.040 / 0.68; UH
0.009 / 0.37 against 0.022 / 0.92; LIST 0.026 / 0.65 against 0.032 / 0.78; and UNEP
0.027 / 0.35 against 0.045 / 0.57. At UH's own list size the geography rule reaches 92%
of the reference damage at more than twice UH's precision. Only two products stay ahead of geography alone: Microsoft (0.081 / 0.55 against
0.053 / 0.36), which shipped only its carefully analysed strip, and OSU (0.036 / 0.85 against
0.032 / 0.77), which flagged so widely it bought recall the null could not match at that list
length. This result is unchanged by the matching radius: repeated at 20 m it is the same four
products, in the same direction (Appendix). One caveat cuts across all
of this: outside Caraballeda the reference is thin, and the penalty for flagging there
falls on the products, which did flag, not on the baseline, which did not. To whatever
extent CEMS under-recorded those areas, part of the gap would close. But a responder in
the first week had exactly the same information deficit, which is the point of the
as-delivered frame.




### The single-product ceiling: three experiments {.unnumbered}

Could a better single product fix per-building precision? Three independent experiments
in this event say no. The limit behaves like a property of the sensing method rather
than of any particular product. We refer to it as the modality ceiling: a precision level
that single-method tuning does not rise above. (Note that this is the opposite kind of
bound from the reference-driven lower bounds of @sec-floor: those mean the truth is
higher than measured; the ceiling means single-product performance stops improving.)

1. **Same-sensor agreement barely helps.** Requiring both Sentinel-1 coherence products
   (IMPACT and OSU) to agree raises precision only to 0.088, barely above the single
   products. Products that share sensor physics share false positives, so voting cannot
   remove them.
2. **Product confidence scores add nothing.** Sweeping Microsoft's continuous
   damage-fraction score (within its own analysed region, where its baseline numbers run
   higher than in the core region) trades recall 0.66→0.10 for precision 0.10→0.19. The
   shipped binary flag already sits near the best F1 on that curve. There is no hidden headroom
   in the confidence field.
3. **Agreement within one product plateaus too.** Microsoft flags corroborated by a
   second satellite scene are 2.5 times more precise than single-scene flags (0.245
   versus 0.097). That is a real gain and worth publishing. But it remains well below the
   strongest two-product rule (0.372), and in the low-damage zone where two scenes overlap, even flags
   confirmed by both scenes were rejected by 72% of crowd reviews. Agreement inside one
   model inherits that model's calibration failures.


### The west-strip case study, in full {.unnumbered}

The scorecard left the Microsoft west-strip anomaly unexplained. It can now be resolved
completely, and the resolution is the paper's best argument for metadata transparency.

The crowd settles what the cluster is. In the western strip, volunteers judged 71% of
Microsoft-flagged locations "no damage", against a roughly even split in the damage-dense
east. Independent people looking at post-event imagery saw nothing at most of the places
the cluster flags. The cluster is real over-detection, not a gap in the reference.

The product's own metadata explains where it came from. Every building in the strip has
`num_observations = 1`: the zone was covered by exactly one satellite scene. The platform
behind the product (HASTE; Robinson, Ortiz et al. 2026) trains a fresh model for each
scene and uses agreement between overlapping scenes as its only internal check. The west
never got that check. Cloud is ruled out as an alternative explanation: the west is the
most cloud-free zone in the product, and the visibility check in Methods moved nothing.
Splitting the product at the scene boundary shows what the headline number was hiding.
The single-scene west flags 28.7% of its buildings, with precision 0.05 and F1 0.10. The
multi-scene east flags 7.6%, with precision 0.21 and F1 0.30, the best single-product
zone we measured anywhere in this study. The same product contains both.

A head-to-head test of the two overlapping scenes pins down the mechanism. Scored
independently on the ~24,700 buildings both scenes covered, the "better" scene's
advantage turns out to be restraint, not accuracy: it flags 4.9% of buildings against the
other's 27.8%, but its flags are crowd-confirmed at a lower rate (7% versus 14%).
Microsoft's merge rule, which resolved conflicts in favour of that scene, was
directionally right (68% of the overruled flags were crowd-rejected) but silently
discarded roughly 845 flags on buildings the crowd judged damaged. And buildings flagged
by both scenes were still 72% crowd-rejected in this low-damage zone. The failure unit is
the calibration of each per-scene model, not the satellite, the provider, or the product
as a whole.

A cross-product control seals that attribution. UH's authors confirm their analysis ran
exclusively on Vantor imagery (the same commercial source as the failing scene) and over
the same strip UH shows the opposite pattern: it flags 3.4% of buildings in the west at
precision 0.138 (its best zone anywhere), against Microsoft's 32.4% at 0.033. Same imagery
vendor, different model, no cluster; the failure travelled with the per-scene calibration,
not the pixels. (UH's acquisition dates are unconfirmed, so this is vendor-level rather
than scene-level evidence.)

Three things about this case study generalize. First, a single product-level metric
averaged over a 4× internal quality split, and the split was only detectable because
per-building provenance was published. Second, the provider's own validation missed the
failure: the failing scene was exactly the one absent from their labeled validation set,
and the platform's previous external evaluation (Turkey) showed the opposite bias,
conservative under-flagging. Per-scene behaviour in a new event was not predictable from
the track record. Third, the diagnosis was available during the response: the crowd
campaign that rejected 71% of the strip's flags finished within days of the flags being
published, but no channel existed to carry that signal to the provider. For the five
products that publish no per-building provenance, we can show that they fail but never
why.

### A version postscript: what a product revision changes

One provider revised its product after the study window: OSU delivered a v1 on 22 July
(confidence tiers, ~8% expanded coverage, 69,431 flags versus v0's 58,870). The paper
scores v0 throughout, because v0 is what responders had during the response; the
operational dashboard has moved to v1. Since both versions key to the same building
base, they can be scored identically on the common extent against the same 1,488 CEMS
points (this comparison spans OSU's full extent, so its precision runs lower than the
core-region scorecard figure). The result: precision 0.036 (v0) versus 0.034 (v1),
recall 0.68 versus 0.64, no measurable accuracy change, while **more than half the flag list turned over** (v1
dropped 30,565 of v0's 57,066 flags and added 42,723 new ones). A revision that
relabels half the buildings without moving precision or recall is itself evidence for
this paper's central reading: at the individual-building level these products are
noise-dominated, and version-to-version stability deserves a place beside accuracy in
how such products are judged. The area-level signal, by contrast, is robust to exactly
this kind of churn.



### Radar and optical: why they fail differently {#sec-sensing .unnumbered}

Optical products (Microsoft, UH) classify what damage looks like from above. Radar
coherence products (IMPACT, OSU) measure something else: whether the fine-scale
arrangement of radar reflectors inside each pixel stayed stable between satellite passes.
An intact building is a stable reflector and keeps high coherence; a collapse rearranges
the reflectors and coherence drops. Vegetation never holds coherence in the first place,
so coherence methods are largely immune to the farmland and vegetation changes that
produce false alarms in optical and amplitude-based methods. LIST also runs on radar,
but not on coherence: per the provider it is a deep-learning change-detection model (a
ResNet) applied to before-and-after radar images (no methodology document accompanied
the delivery), so we do not assume it shares that protection. UNEP's debris mass is
likewise radar-derived.

The contrast is measurable in this event. Santa Cruz serves as a control case: the
expert reference analysed it and found almost no damage, and much of it is agricultural.
There the two coherence products flagged 1.2% and 0.9% of buildings, while the optical
UH product flagged 27.5% (@sec-floor).

### Performance versus matching radius {.unnumbered}

All CEMS-based results in this paper use a 10 m matching radius, and every model is
fitted and evaluated at that radius. Because the radius defines the target itself, the
whole analysis is re-run at 20 m (doubling the positive class: 2,733 labelled buildings
against 1,350) and at 30 m (the line-of-sight scale), and @tbl-radii shows every
predictor at every radius, measured by one machinery throughout.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-radii
#| tbl-cap: "Precision, recall, and F1 for every product and model at matching radii of 10, 20, and 30 m. Each cell shows the core-region value with the as-delivered value in parentheses (products only: the as-delivered geography benchmark is refit per product footprint, so the models have no single as-delivered number). Cell shading ranks the CORE values within each column, darker = higher. Products are scored at their shipped operating point, models at their best single cut."
import pandas as pd
from great_tables import GT, style, loc
from matplotlib import colormaps
from matplotlib.colors import to_hex

core = {r: pd.read_csv(f"artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/rq8_best_f1_r{r}.csv").set_index("predictor")
        for r in (10, 20, 30)}
asd = {r: pd.read_csv(f"artefacts/RQ8-learned-fusion/rq8b_asdelivered_baseline_r{r}.csv").set_index("product")
       for r in (10, 20, 30)}
for r in asd:
    a = asd[r]
    a["f1"] = 2 * a.P_product * a.R_product / (a.P_product + a.R_product)

rows = [("MS", "MS", "Microsoft"), ("IMPACT", "IMPACT", "IMPACT v2"), ("OSU", "OSU", "OSU"),
        ("UH", "UH", "UH"), ("LIST", "LIST", "LIST"), ("UNEP", "UNEP", "UNEP"),
        ("geography null (logistic)", None, "geography null (logistic)"),
        ("geography null (rand. forest)", None, "geography null (random forest)"),
        ("flat k-of-6 voting", None, "flat k-of-6 voting"),
        ("weighted fusion", None, "weighted fusion")]
metrics = [("precision", "P_product", "P"), ("recall", "R_product", "R"), ("f1", "f1", "F1")]

disp, nums = [], []
for key, akey, label in rows:
    d = {"predictor": label}; n = {}
    for r in (10, 20, 30):
        c = core[r].loc[key]
        for m, am, ml in metrics:
            col = f"{ml}{r}"
            n[col] = float(c[m])
            if akey is not None:
                d[col] = f"{c[m]:.3f} ({float(asd[r].loc[akey][am]):.3f})"
            else:
                d[col] = f"{c[m]:.3f}"
    disp.append(d); nums.append(n)
df = pd.DataFrame(disp)
nm = pd.DataFrame(nums)

cmap = colormaps["Blues"]
gt = (GT(df)
      .tab_spanner("10 m", [c for c in df.columns if c.endswith("10")])
      .tab_spanner("20 m", [c for c in df.columns if c.endswith("20")])
      .tab_spanner("30 m", [c for c in df.columns if c.endswith("30")])
      .cols_label(**{f"{ml}{r}": ml for r in (10, 20, 30) for _, _, ml in metrics}))
for col in nm.columns:
    lo, hi = nm[col].min(), nm[col].max()
    for i2 in range(len(nm)):
        f = 0.0 if hi == lo else (nm[col][i2] - lo) / (hi - lo)
        gt = gt.tab_style(style.fill(color=to_hex(cmap(0.08 + 0.34 * f))),
                          loc.body(columns=col, rows=[i2]))
gt
```

Three patterns to read from it. Every number rises with the radius, because a flag one
or two buildings away from recorded damage starts to count as a hit. The geography null
gains fastest: a wider radius smears each expert point into a blob of neighbouring
buildings, making the target area-shaped, which is exactly the shape a smooth spatial
predictor captures well, and by 30 m the null's F1 matches or beats five of the six
products. And combination stays ahead at every radius (voting 0.290/0.342/0.364, fusion
0.343/0.386/0.427), so the paper's conclusions do not depend on the radius choice; the
tight 10 m label is simply the most demanding reading, and the one where a building-level
claim means a building. The wider radius raises all absolute values,
because a flag one building away from a recorded damage point starts to count as a hit. It
also flatters the geography null specifically, for a reason worth understanding: a wide radius
smears each reference point into a blob of neighbouring buildings, making the target
area-shaped, which is exactly the shape a smooth spatial predictor captures well. The tighter
10 m label concentrates the positives onto individual buildings, where per-building
discrimination is required, and there the case for *combining* products strengthens, from 1.8×
to 2.3× the best single product. Reporting at 10 m is therefore both the more consistent choice
and the more demanding one.

A second implementation check belongs beside this one. The headline scorecard matches
flags to CEMS points on each product's native geometry, while the fusion analysis matches
by building centroid; a reader could reasonably worry that this difference alone shifts
the numbers. It does not: at the same 10 m radius the two implementations agree to
within 0.005 for every product:

| product | scorecard (native geometry) | fusion analysis (centroid) | difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| UH | 0.090 | 0.093 | +0.003 |
| UNEP | 0.090 | 0.086 | −0.004 |
| Microsoft | 0.080 | 0.081 | +0.001 |
| IMPACT | 0.070 | 0.069 | −0.001 |
| LIST | 0.060 | 0.057 | −0.003 |
| OSU | 0.040 | 0.045 | +0.005 |

: Precision at r = 10 m under the two matching implementations. Centroid versus
native-geometry matching is worth at most 0.005; with the radius held fixed the two are
effectively the same measurement. {#tbl-frames}

**The per-building visibility (cloud) check.** Only Microsoft publishes a per-building
visibility field. Scored against it, the effect is negligible in this event: 3.6% of
buildings are mostly obscured, precision is unchanged under any visibility filter, and
exactly one missed reference point falls on an obscured building. The model abstains
under cloud rather than flagging into it.

### Was the model-versus-product comparison fair? {.unnumbered}

This section carries the machinery behind @sec-null's fairness claims, for the reader
who wants to check them.

**Which learner represents geography best.** Every feature set is fitted with both a
class-balanced logistic regression and a random forest (400 trees, minimum leaf 20), and
the stronger one is reported:

| feature set | random forest | logistic |
|---|---|---|
| all inputs (weighted fusion) | 0.283 | 0.284 |
| context only, core region | 0.045 | **0.060** |
| context only, full delivered footprints | **stronger for 5 of 6** | stronger for MS only |
| products only | 0.258 | 0.271 |

: Average precision by learner and feature set, under spatially blocked validation. Where
products are involved the learner is irrelevant; for the geography null it is not, and
which learner wins depends on the analysis layer. {#tbl-learners}

Wherever products enter, the two learners are indistinguishable, so no fusion result
depends on the choice. The null is a different matter, and the two analysis layers
disagree about which model represents geography better. In the compact core region the
logistic wins (0.060 against 0.045): shaking is near-constant there and the remaining
relationship is smooth, so the forest mostly fits block-specific structure that does not
generalise. Across the full delivered footprints the ranking reverses for five of six
products, because those regions span real variation in shaking that interacts
non-linearly with coast distance and density. The paper therefore uses the logistic null
in the core region and the forest null in the as-delivered analysis: the
report-the-stronger rule applied twice. One further reporting detail: the headline fusion
number comes from the logistic regression, which scores identically to the forest (AP
0.28 either way), while the null and its products-only mirror are both fitted with the
forest so that those two are directly comparable to each other.

**How much event information the null uses, by analysis layer.** Within the compact
core region the ShakeMap estimate barely varies and its measured importance is exactly
0.000: there the null runs on coastline distance and building density alone, and its
skill is a hindsight description of where damage happened to fall. Across the full
delivered footprints, shaking varies for real and carries 0.25–0.31 of the model's
weight, so the null genuinely uses event information there. Microsoft is the exception
that proves the mechanism: it shipped only the coastal strip, and over that
near-identical ground the shaking term again drops to zero.

**Coefficients and thresholds are protected separately.** The model's coefficients are
estimated strictly out-of-fold: each building's score comes from a model that never saw
its block. The decision threshold (the cut that turns the continuous risk into a flag
list) is a second, separate choice that blocked validation does nothing to protect, so
where a single operating point is reported the cut is selected inside the training folds
and applied blind to the held-out data. The difference this makes here is nil (F1 0.129
with the cut chosen out-of-sample against 0.128 chosen in hindsight), but that is a fact
about this sample size (a single scalar estimated from hundreds of thousands of
buildings is pinned down closely either way), not a general licence: on a small reference
the same shortcut could flatter a model materially.

**Why a single product's average precision is degenerate.** Average precision is a
recall-weighted sum over the steps of a precision–recall curve, and a binary flag list
has only two steps: the flagged set itself, and the trivial "flag everything" endpoint.
It therefore evaluates to
$$\mathrm{AP}_{\text{binary}} = P\cdot R + (1-R)\cdot \pi$$
where $\pi$ is the prevalence of damage. The second term is free credit that any
predictor whatsoever collects for the flag-everything endpoint. Because $\pi$ (0.023
here) is far below every product's precision, the term drags each product's AP down
toward prevalence, hardest for the products with the lowest recall. The effect is to
compress genuinely different products into a narrow band (0.042–0.055 across our six,
whose precisions actually range from 0.045 to 0.093), sitting right where a mediocre
continuous score also lands (the forest null's AP is 0.045). Two products can share an
AP because one has high precision and low recall while the other has the reverse; the
number conceals exactly the trade-off an operational reader cares about. This is why the
paper reports AP only among the continuous scores and places the products as points,
never as AP bars beside them.

![Why as-delivered precision falls the way it does. Each product's as-delivered precision
(y) is plotted against the share of its flags that land outside Caraballeda (x), where the
reference records essentially no damage. Every product lies on the diagonal (precision
lost equals the share of flags in the dead zones), so the as-delivered precision is
governed almost entirely by *where* a product chose to flag, not by any resistance to false
alarms. Microsoft is spared only because it flagged nowhere else. This is the arithmetic
behind the first mechanism in
@sec-floor.](artefacts/RQ2-cems-footprint-points/figs/rq2m_deadzone_dilution.png){#fig-deadzone}

### How the crowd adjustment works, and what happened when the crowd voted again {.unnumbered}

Every crowd-adjusted precision in this paper comes from one simple rule, and
@fig-crowdmech shows it acting on a real street in Catia La Mar. A flagged building with
an expert damage point within 10 m counts as a hit outright; the crowd plays no part in
that. Every other flag sits inside one of the ~50 m cells that MapSwipe volunteers voted
on, and the rule is: if most volunteers who saw that cell said *yes, damaged*, the flag is
counted as confirmed damage and improves the adjusted precision; if they said *no* or *not
sure*, it stays a false alarm. Flags in cells the volunteers never saw are assumed to
contain damage at the same rate as the flags the volunteers did see.

In August 2026, after this paper's numbers were frozen, the campaign over this strip was
run a second time: 728 new volunteers re-judged exactly the same 3,482 cells, and each
cell now received about sixteen votes instead of six. Same buildings, different people, a
much harder look. Two caveats keep this from being a perfect replication. The answer
buttons changed: round 2 offered no "no damage" option, so a volunteer who saw nothing
wrong had to press "not sure", which means round 1's headline finding for this strip
(71% of cells actively judged undamaged) simply cannot be re-measured. And the two rounds
showed volunteers different, though similarly dated, satellite images.

What can be compared across the rounds is how much damage the crowd *confirmed*, and that
held up. Of Microsoft's 7,661 flags in this strip with no expert match, the first crowd
confirmed 13.2%; the second, deeper-looking crowd confirmed 11.5%. Two independent juries
agree that roughly one flag in eight has crowd-visible damage under it. If anything, the
harder look confirmed slightly *less*, so the crowd-adjusted values in this paper should
be read as sitting a little high, consistent with their stated role as upper estimates.

What did not hold up is *which* cells were confirmed: only about a quarter of the cells
the first crowd confirmed were confirmed again by the second (the purple outlines in
@fig-crowdmech). That sounds alarming until one asks how much two small juries should
agree even if volunteers were perfectly consistent, and the answer is: not much. Six
votes on a borderline cell is close to a coin toss, and once that known voting noise is
accounted for, the two rounds' underlying judgements agree well (correlation 0.63, versus
0.29 before the correction). Most of the apparent chaos is small vote counts, not fickle
volunteers. The practical lesson is the one this paper already follows: a single cell's
verdict is too noisy to lean on, but sums over thousands of cells are steady, which is
why crowd verdicts appear here only inside aggregate numbers, never as building-level
ground truth.

Finally, the cost in numbers. Recomputing each product's crowd-adjusted precision with the
second round's verdicts in place of the first moves it by at most 0.03 in either
direction: Microsoft's falls from 0.237 to 0.223, UNEP's from 0.074 to 0.043 (nearly all
of its crowd-reviewed flags sit in this one strip), and IMPACT's and UH's tick slightly
upward. No product overtakes another.

![How the MapSwipe crowd enters the precision calculation, and what an independent re-vote
changed. Both panels show the same Catia La Mar neighbourhood; hexagons are the ~50 m crowd
task cells, tinted by majority verdict. **A**, round 1: a flag matched by an expert point
within 10 m is a true positive (green); an unmatched flag in a cell the crowd judged
damaged is counted as confirmed and improves the adjusted precision (blue); in a cell
judged undamaged or uncertain it remains a false alarm (orange). **B**, round 2, re-voted
the identical cells at ~16 votes each, with no "no damage" answer available (its "not
sure" absorbs it): purple outlines mark cells whose verdict changed sides. Individual
cells flip; the total the adjustment depends on barely moves (13.2% → 11.5% of the
strip's unmatched Microsoft flags confirmed).](artefacts/RQ7-mapswipe-validation/figs/rq7_crowd_adjustment_explainer.png){#fig-crowdmech}


## Reproducibility note {.unnumbered}

All analyses run from immutable data snapshots, frozen on 2026-07-15 and stored as
Parquet, GeoParquet, CSV, and GeoJSON files in the project's Azure blob storage.
Per-question scripts, running notes, and the full findings register, including every
negative and superseded result, accompany this draft in the project repository.
